question: A matrix $A$ has order $2\times3$. Examine whether an inverse of $A$ can exist under matrix multiplication. Justify your answer using the orders of the required products.
explanation:
Possible order of a multiplying matrix
For $AB$ to be defined as a square matrix, $B$ would have to be of order $3\times2$, giving $AB$ of order $2\times2$.
Reverse product
With the same $B$, the product $BA$ would have order $3\times3$. Thus, $AB$ and $BA$ cannot both be the same identity matrix.
Existence of inverse
An inverse under matrix multiplication requires $AB=BA=I$ for square matrices of the same order. Therefore, the rectangular matrix $A$ does not possess an inverse.

options.A: Yes. A $2\times3$ matrix can have an inverse of order $3\times2$ because both products have order $2\times2$.
options.B: Yes. Any rectangular matrix has an inverse if all its entries are non-zero.
options.C: No. With $B$ of order $3\times2$, $AB$ is $2\times2$ while $BA$ is $3\times3$, so a two-sided inverse of $A$ cannot exist.
options.D: No. The product of a $2\times3$ matrix with any matrix is never defined.
